summary: This RFC defines X.509 extended key purpose identifiers for general-purpose and trust anchor configuration files, for software and firmware update packages, and for safety-critical communication. These identifiers limit what a certificate may be used for.

plainLanguage.summary: A key can be marked "opens only the supply door." This adds new labels for certificates that sign updates, settings, or safety-critical messages.

questions: extended key usage for firmware updates
how to restrict a certificate to firmware signing
subtitle: Four new certificate labels that say a key may sign configs, trust anchors, updates, or secure safety-critical links.

tldr.problem: A certificate with no restriction, or with a generic purpose such as code signing, could be misused, for example to sign a trust anchor configuration file that a device then accepts.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9809 defines four Extended Key Usage purpose identifiers: id-kp-configSigning, id-kp-trustAnchorConfigSigning, id-kp-updatePackageSigning and id-kp-safetyCommunication, with OIDs 41 to 44 under the PKIX id-kp arc.
tldr.outcome: Systems can require the matching purpose before trusting a signed file or a safety-critical peer. The identifiers reduce existing risks and do not add new ones.

today: RFC 9809 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2025. It is not obsoleted or updated by any other RFC and builds on the EKU extension of RFC 5280.

sections.title: Why New Key Purposes Are Needed
sections.content:
The Extended Key Usage (EKU) extension of an X.509 certificate lists KeyPurposeIds that express the intended purpose of the key for humans and complying libraries. The list is kept in the IANA registry 'SMI Security for PKIX Extended Key Purpose'. Using anyExtendedKeyUsage is generally considered poor practice.

If a certificate's purpose is not restricted, the risk of cross-application attacks rises. The RFC's example is trust anchor management: a device could accept a trust anchor configuration file signed by a service whose certificate has no EKU, or has id-kp-codeSigning or id-kp-documentSigning (RFC 9336). A device should only accept such files if the signer's certificate was explicitly issued for that purpose.

There were also no KeyPurposeIds for safety-critical communication. Vendor-defined identifiers can cause interoperability problems outside their environment or when marked critical, so the RFC defines standard ones.
sections.plainLanguage: If any key could sign anything, a sneaky helper could change the house rules. Marking keys for one job each stops that.

sections.title: The Four Key Purposes
sections.content:
The RFC defines four KeyPurposeIds:

  • id-kp-configSigning: signing general-purpose configuration files (for example XML, YAML or JSON), which configure hardware or software.
  • id-kp-trustAnchorConfigSigning: signing trust anchor configuration files, which add or remove trust anchors in a device's trust store.
  • id-kp-updatePackageSigning: signing software or firmware update packages, including bootloader, firmware and safety-related applications.
  • id-kp-safetyCommunication: authenticating a communication peer for safety-critical communication based on TLS or other protocols.

'Safety-critical communication' means communication that could, under certain conditions, lead to a state in which human life, health, property or the environment is endangered.

The definitions are intentionally broad. They were initially motivated by industrial automation and rail automation, but details for each deployment belong in the relevant technical standards and certificate policies.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four tags: 'may sign settings', 'may sign trust-list changes', 'may sign updates', and 'may be trusted for safety talk'.

sections.title: How Verifiers and Requesters Use Them
sections.content:
Per RFC 5280, if the EKU extension is present the certificate MUST only be used for one of the indicated purposes. The four new identifiers are not intrinsically mutually exclusive. Which combinations are acceptable is left to the technical standard of the application and the certificate policy of the PKI. The RFC gives examples, such as a standard saying a relying party must ignore id-kp-trustAnchorConfigSigning when id-kp-safetyCommunication is present.

Systems that verify these signatures or authenticate safety peers SHOULD require the corresponding KeyPurposeId in the EKU. If the certificate requester knows users are mandated to use them, it MUST enforce their inclusion, and MUST ensure the Key Usage extension is set to digitalSignature for signature verification, keyEncipherment for public key encryption, and keyAgreement for key agreement.
sections.plainLanguage: A device should look for the right tag before trusting a signature. Which tags may share a key is decided by the local rules.

sections.title: Encoding in Certificates and the ASN.1 Module
sections.content:
The EKU extension is ExtKeyUsageSyntax ::= SEQUENCE SIZE (1..MAX) OF KeyPurposeId, where a KeyPurposeId is an object identifier. The extension may be critical or non-critical at the issuer's option. It applies to end-entity certificates and can be used together with the Key Usage extension.

The new identifiers sit under the PKIX id-kp arc, { iso(1) identified-organization(3) dod(6) internet(1) security(5) mechanisms(5) pkix(7) 3 }, as values 41, 42, 43 and 44. Appendix A gives the ASN.1 module, named id-mod-config-update-sc-eku with module number 117.

A certification authority must make sure correct EKU and KU values go into each certificate. Including these identifiers does not preclude including other KeyPurposeIds.
sections.plainLanguage: Each tag is really a long number written in a standard way, so every computer reads it the same.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 5280 apply. The RFC says these purposes do not introduce new risks but reduce existing ones by identifying what a certificate was generated for.

To limit cross-protocol attacks, a relying party may prohibit specific combinations of KeyPurposeIds, using the excluded and permitted KeyPurposeId procedure in Section 4 of RFC 9336. An example exclusion is anyExtendedKeyUsage; an example allowed combination is id-kp-safetyCommunication with id-kp-clientAuth or id-kp-serverAuth.

On privacy, certificates are sent in the clear in some protocols such as TLS 1.2 and encrypted in others such as TLS 1.3. An EKU can help an observer or, through Certificate Transparency logs for publicly issued certificates, an attacker infer a certificate's purpose, which may reveal private information about the subject.
sections.plainLanguage: The tags make things safer, but a tag also tells a snooper what a key is for, so that can leak a little.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA registered the module OID 117 (id-mod-config-update-sc-eku) in the 'SMI Security for PKIX Module Identifier' registry. It also registered four purposes in the 'SMI Security for PKIX Extended Key Purpose' registry: 41 id-kp-configSigning, 42 id-kp-trustAnchorConfigSigning, 43 id-kp-updatePackageSigning and 44 id-kp-safetyCommunication.
sections.plainLanguage: The four tag numbers were written down in the official public list.

sections.title: Motivating Use Cases
sections.content:
Appendix B, which is informational, describes automation products that must meet cybersecurity requirements such as the European Union Cyber Resilience Act. It says products connected to the Internet and sold in the EU after 2027 must bear the CE marking to show compliance. Standardized attributes would give transparency and interoperability for updates, configuration, trust anchor configuration and safety-critical communication across vendors.

A concrete example is a rail automation system, citing the Europe's Rail System Pillar, which aims at a unified operational concept and a safe and secure system architecture for the European heavy rail network.
sections.plainLanguage: Trains and factories use gear from many makers, so they all need to agree on the same tags.
